old/information-kalman-filter.html.title: Information Kalman Filter
old/information-kalman-filter.html.description:
Based on Gaussian Information Aggregation, assume that we have two sources of information. Process/prediction Equation Sensor/observation Equation We desire to obtain an estimation of , , based on the information provided by the estimate of and estimate of measurements , inputs at two consecutive time steps , and of the modelling errors and . We asume that the knowledge that we have about these variables is statistical even if the underlying physical variable is deterministic ( perspective that we adopt): Noise is Gaussian white, and different noise sources are independent:
We cast these equations so they resemble the form used in Old/Gaussian Information Aggregation Lemma: So, for the process equation:Note that the measurement is obtained through the filter itself, and therefore it is the estimation of the Kalman filter at , : That is, a stochastic variable. Analogously, is the measurement of the input, so it is in general stochastic. Therefore: From which:Notice that is the information coming from the use of the prediction equation; this is addressed making to make explicit the origin of the information.The sensor equation is reordered as: so,Therefore: From which:Notice that is the information coming from the use of the observation equation; this is addressed making to make explicit the origin of the information.Finally, the estimate is: In summary: from which If ( has maximum row rank), then:Notice that this is the estimation of the projection of the state onto the row space of (see figure):
The figure depicts the projection of the state () onto the hyperplane (greenish) expanded by the row space of (). In this way, the estimator can be said to be: "The FIM weighted average of the estimations of the prediction and observation estimations." We can retrieve this interpretation when by splitting the set of observation equations into subsets:where have each one maximum row rank. Now we have several sources of information to aggregate: For each of them Therefore from which Note also that even if , we can write: This equation is a very convenient form to look at the sensor fusion, as it allows to integrate sensors separating them into groups. This can be of interest when having different frequencies for different measurements or predictions of states, or when a sensor or prediction equation may fail. It also makes easy the parallel computation or distribution of the measurements and predictions on different nodes. This robustifies the setup because it easily allows removing different sources of information if they are not available.

We explicitly define the statistical properties of our estimators and physical modeling errors as Gaussian random variables: We assume strictly that noise is Gaussian white, and all different noise sources and estimators are mutually independent:

Analogously, is the stochastic measurement of the input).Evaluating the expected estimator for this source, the unknown zero-mean noise drops out, yielding the prediction estimator:While its corresponding variance strictly retains the noise:From which the Information components for the prediction are naturally defined:We reorder the physical sensor equation to isolate the state term:We define our second information source () by replacing the physical parameters with our estimators, retaining the unmodeled sensor noise :Evaluating the expected estimator, the zero-mean noise drops out, yielding the estimator of the projected state:And its variance expands to:From which the Information components for the observation are naturally defined:

For each subset : Therefore, the information matrices and vectors are defined as: From which the aggregated total is evaluated: Note also that even if , we can always write: This equation is a very convenient form to look at the sensor fusion, as it allows to integrate sensors separating them into groups. This can be of interest when having different frequencies for different measurements or predictions of states, or when a sensor or prediction equation may fail. It also makes easy the parallel computation or distribution of the measurements and predictions on different nodes. This robustifies the setup because it easily allows removing different sources of information if they are not available.Standard Kalman Filter literature frequently assumes that the control input is purely deterministic (zero variance) or lacks a direct feedthrough matrix in the sensor model (). notation-guide-for-information-kalman-fi.title: Notation Guide for Information Kalman Filter Framework
notation-guide-for-information-kalman-fi.description:
This document defines the strict notational conventions used across the Gaussian Information Aggregation framework. The notation is deliberately designed to separate deterministic physical reality from the stochastic estimators used to track it, adhering strictly to a Maximum Likelihood (ML) perspective.In this framework, the true physical state of the system is deterministic (it exists perfectly in reality, even if we don't know what it is). We do not treat the true state as a random variable. Randomness only exists in our sensors, our unmodeled physical disturbances, and the estimators we build from them.
Standard math font (): Denotes the true, deterministic physical quantities.
The "Hat" (): Denotes a stochastic estimator or measurement of a physical quantity. Because it is derived from noisy data, any variable with a hat is rigorously treated as a random variable.
The framework linearizes nonlinear systems into matrices (Jacobians). Physical disturbances and sensor inaccuracies are modeled as zero-mean Gaussian white noise.To unify the treatment of predictions and observations, any equation that provides mathematical insight into the state is generalized as an "Information Source" (). We make a strict distinction between the abstract random variable (which retains physical noise to facilitate variance/correlation expansion) and its evaluated estimator (which drops the zero-mean noise for numerical computation).Example Definitions (Prediction):
The Source: The Estimator: The framework uses standard covariance definitions alongside Fisher Information operators. The subscript of a covariance matrix dictates the random variables being evaluated.When information sources are correlated (), they cannot be directly added. The framework uses the Schur complement to orthogonalize one source with respect to the other prior to additive fusion. The "Tilde" ( ) denotes these decorrelated, orthogonalized quantities.

epistemic-interpretation-of-the-kalman-f.title: Epistemic Interpretation of the Kalman Filter Process Equation
epistemic-interpretation-of-the-kalman-f.description:
1. Ontological View of the Process Equation(Note: $\mathbf{f}{\mathbf{u}} \mathbf{u}k$ is temporarily omitted for simplification)In this view, the equation represents a single realization of an experiment; the variables are therefore the "true" variables in that particular realization.Here, is random, meaning that in a particular realization it assumes a concrete physical value, and thus the single-realization view of the equation is maintained. However, different realizations will present different values of . Consequently, across different realizations, will have different "random" values. This randomness is driven entirely by physical variations in .In this context, the initial state at may be known exactly. This paradigm fully captures the reality of classical processes, where can be interpreted as physical modeling errors or sources of noise external to the system. Even though these sources are real and deterministic at a micro-level, they are practically unknowable to us.The Problem of InferenceThe problem of how to perform inference with this formula begins as soon as we concede:
"We don't know the exact " "We don't know the exact " The only things we know about the noise and the initial state are their statistical properties, such as their probability density functions (pdf). For instance:From here, we can begin to make statistical inferences. If is independent with respect to (meaning that across any realization of the experiment, the noise is not related to the state ), then from the process equation ():If we expand this to the next step ():In this case, we have a precise statistical description of . This description is firmly attached to physical "reality" because we assume that the distributions assigned to and represent the actual frequency of those values across real experiments. Therefore, our ontological view of the process equation leads to an ontological statistical description of the states, anchored in physical reality.2. The Epistemic Shift (Knowledge View)Alternatively, we can adopt a different view, one in which (for instance):are random variables representing our knowledge of through a particular pdf.In this context the true variable mus be differentiated from the random variable representing it knowledge such as in:
The underlying true state could, in fact, be a deterministic constant independent of the realization—meaning true reality is . However, because we do not know it, our description reflects our idea or knowledge of the state rather than the physical reality itself. This is an epistemic view.In this case, the statistical statements and equations from the previous section still hold mathematically true. However, their interpretation shifts entirely. The pdf of (and consequently or ) no longer represents the statistical distribution of the true variable across different physical experiments (the ontological view). Instead, it represents the degree of knowledge we currently possess about the variable. This knowledge lives within our algorithm; and no longer need to be statistically measurable physical quantities, but rather parameters of our belief.This epistemic paradigm proves to be more general than the ontological one. If the statistics we assign to and happen to correspond exactly to physical reality, then the resulting distributions for and will perfectly match the statistical reality of the real experiments. Conversely, if they are strictly a "measure of belief" not rooted in a physical distribution (e.g., assuming a deterministic state is a random variable simply because we lack better information), then the computed distributions for and will seamlessly track the evolution of that knowledge.3. Showing the Paradox with Deterministic InputsAssume that temperature enters the system. Temperature exists as a deterministic physical variable, but the sensor measuring it is affected by randomness (as with many physical sensors).If the temperature enters the process equation as an input:(Where Measured Temperature)Our best knowledge of the true input is characterized by the sensor noise: . Once this is introduced, the inference regarding the statistical description of is no longer purely physical. The true temperature is deterministic, but to perform mathematical inference, we must treat as a random variable.Even if the state's true physical variation is only , our best possible inference of the covariance () must now include the uncertainty of the sensor:4. Conclusion: Reconciling the ViewsIf we set aside quantum physics (where we might argue that reality occupies multiple states simultaneously with a given pdf) and restrict ourselves to the classical macroscopic view of the physical world, the true state and true noise are unique for each realization. This remains true regardless of whether the uncertainty enters via the physical process () or simply through the sensor measurement ().At a conceptual level, in this classical context, the Ontological and Engineering views coincide. The true philosophical distinction lies between this Engineering/Ontological view (where randomness is strictly quantified by physically knowledgeable accounts of noise sources) and the Epistemic view.The Epistemic view is ultimately superior because:As demonstrated, the moment measurement noise on a deterministic input enters the process equation, it acts as an epistemic source of uncertainty. Therefore, when adopting th epistemic view, we will say that the true process equation is:
To which corresponds the "epistemic" equation
Here we consistently treat , and as a set of random variables that epistemically reflect our knowledge of reality. This holds true whether that knowledge is derived from a precise, physically-based statistical description of process noise , a sensor measurement with known statistical properties, or our inference of the initial state .The epistemic view reconciles all perspectives and serves as the most general framework. It allows us to interpret our predictions as the absolute best estimates available—whether they are based on precise physical characterizations or simply the best bounds of our current knowledge.5. The Epistemic View of the Sensor EquationTo complete this framework, we apply the same epistemic lens to the sensor equation. Here, we deviate from the standard Kalman filter literature to establish a more rigorous distinction between hardware noise and modeling error.Let the true physical sensor relationship be:To which corresponds our epistemic equation:Under this epistemic interpretation, the variables take on a very specific meaning: is a random variable representing our knowledge of the sensor measurement. Because it represents the sensor reading, its statistical variance explicitly captures the physical hardware noise of the sensor. , therefore, is not the raw sensor noise. Instead, it represents the sensor equation noise. It encapsulates our epistemic uncertainty regarding the measurement model itself—such as an imperfect mathematical representation of the sensor's physical mounting, unmodeled environmental perturbations, or geometric simplifications in . By isolating the hardware noise within and the model uncertainty within , we establish a natural bridge to the Information Filter perspective. The sensor equation is no longer viewed merely as a forward prediction of a reading, but as an explicit source of inference for the state. By rearranging the equation, we can isolate the informational contribution provided by the sensor:This formulation explicitly demonstrates that our updated knowledge of the observed state components () is epistemically derived: we take our noisy measurement knowledge () and subtract our uncertain knowledge of both the deterministic inputs () and the flaws in our own modeling framework ().

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.

info_allowResizing.description: Whether or not to allow the sidebars to be resized

info_allowCollapsing.description: Whether or not to allow the sidebars to be collapsed

info_rightDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the right sidebar

info_leftDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the left sidebar

info_selector.description: CSS selector for an element. The feature will be placed relative to this element.

info_type.description: Will this feature be placed before, after, or inside (at the beggining or end).

info_featurePlacement.description: Where to place this feature on the page. (Relative to the selector)

info_sourcePath.description: The local path to the source .html file which will be included.

info_allowFoldingLists.description: Whether or not to allow lists to be folded

info_allowFoldingHeadings.description: Whether or not to allow headings to be folded

info_siteUrl.description: The url that this site will be hosted at

info_authorName.description: The name of the author of the site
